newsitem.title: UK: EMS/Mark retreats from highs set after French vote.
newsitem.headline: EMS/Mark retreats from highs set after French vote.

text.p: The mark had retreated by European midsession from the highs it jumped to against the French franc after the left swept to victory in weekend elections in France.

The franc initially fell to its lowest level this year amid concern the new government will loosen fiscal policy. Expectations the government will also push for a broad European economic and monetary union drove the mark back from its highs on its European crosses, however.

The German government's plans to revalue Bundesbank assets in a bid to qualify for EMU despite opposition from the central bank has also fanned talk of a broad EMU and is expected to weigh on the mark.
The German currency is not expected to fall too far, though, given persistent speculation that these difficulties could lead to a delay in launching the European single currency, analysts said.
"The Socialist victory and the German plans to revalue gold hints at a broad EMU and this is not bad for the high yielders," said David Coleman, chief international economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"But it also throws the bigger issue of whether EMU will go ahead into a gloomier light so people aren't quite sure how to interpret the French results."

The mark rose as high as 3.3860 French francs, its strongest since December 11, and was last at 3.3808/12 at 1030 GMT from 3.3774/79 late Friday in Europe. It was last at 989.80/10 lire and 84.65/66 from 991.15/65 and 84.66/67 late Friday.
Francois Hollande, a spokesman for the victorious French Socialists, called Monday for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU and said all stood to benefit if Europe "no longer means austerity."

Expectations of a broad EMU also grew after the French Communist Party, on whom the Socialists depend for their parliamentary majority, said their support was conditional on a loosening of the Maastricht convergence criteria.
The German government is expected by traders to resist moves to a broad EMU. Its ability to do so is, however, being limited by its clash with the Bundesbank.
"The market seems to think that EMU will go ahead, but that the euro will be a soft currency," said Robert Prior-Wandesforde, an economist at HSBC Markets.
Still, the mark will get a filip if comments from Bundesbank or German government officials indicate they would prefer to delay the launch of the single currency than to accept a broad EMU.
The Bundesbank denied a report in Germany's Der Spiegel magazine which said German central bank president Hans Tietmeyer had proposed delaying EMU.

Traders will be looking for direction to speeches later today by Bundesbank council members Hans-Juergen Koebnick and Helmut Hesse and by German finance minister Theo Waigel. -- Swaha Pattanaik, London Forex Desk +44 171 542 6284
